results.title: US Auto Parts Tariffs in 2026: Critical Buyer Guide
results.content:
## The Current Tariff Structure

As of 2026, most passenger vehicles and auto parts entering the US are subject to a 25% Section 232 tariff, applied on national security grounds. This rate applies broadly — to major exporting countries like Germany, Japan, and South Korea — unless the goods qualify for a specific exemption. [...] A declining offset for US-assembled vehicles.Automakers assembling vehicles in the US can apply for a partial offset against tariffs paid on imported parts, based on a percentage of the vehicle’s MSRP. This offset was set at 3.75% through April 2026 and has since stepped down to 2.5%, with a full phase-out planned by mid-2027 — a sign that the program is designed as a temporary transition tool rather than a permanent subsidy. [...] Key exemption: Parts and vehicles that qualify under USMCA rules of origin — meaning they meet North American content requirements — continue to enter at a 0% rate from Canada and Mexico. This exemption has become one of the most valuable compliance tools available to importers who can restructure sourcing to qualify.

results.title: Importing Auto Parts into US: 2026 Section 232 Guide
results.content:
Most auto parts imported into the US in 2026 face a 25 percent Section 232 tariff that took effect May 3, 2025. The tariff applies to engines, engine parts, transmissions, powertrain components, and electrical components for passenger vehicles and light trucks, regardless of country of origin. USMCA-qualifying parts from Canada and Mexico are exempt or partially exempt during a transition period. results.title: Section 232 Tariffs on Auto Parts: What U.S. Importers Need to Know in 2026 | Accrue Global Services
results.content:
China — Full Section 232 tariffs apply, stacked on top of Section 301 tariffs. Total effective rates on steel and aluminum auto parts from China often exceed 40%.
 Japan, Taiwan, Vietnam, India — Full Section 232 rates apply with no quota arrangement as of 2026. [...] Section 232 tariffs have been reshaping auto parts imports since 2018 — and in 2026, they are broader, stricter, and more expensive than most importers realize. If you ship performance parts, aftermarket components, suspension systems, or raw materials into the USA, understanding exactly how Section 232 applies to your shipments is not optional. Getting it wrong means paying 25% more than you budgeted, or worse, a CBP penalty you did not see coming. [...] This means the country your parts ship from is not always the country that determines your tariff rate. The country where the steel or aluminum was melted and poured is what matters for Section 232 purposes — the country of origin of the raw material, not the finished part. Transshipment through a third country does not change this.
